The University of Sheffield is a remarkable place to work. Our people are at the heart of everything we do. Their diverse backgrounds, abilities and beliefs make Sheffield a world-class university.

We offer a fantastic range of benefits including a highly competitive annual leave entitlement (with the ability to purchase more), a generous pensions scheme, flexible working opportunities, a commitment to your development and wellbeing, a wide range of retail discounts, and much more. Find out more about our benefits (opens in a new window) and join us to become part of something special.

 

Overview

Applications are invited for a Knowledge Transfer Partnership (KTP) research associate to develop an intelligent weld fabrication platform that can be applied to fabrication projects supported by Building Information Modelling (BIM) and Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) digital twins, delivering market-leading insights to improve fabrication planning, decision-making and productivity.

This is a unique opportunity at the interface of academic research and industrial innovation to develop cutting-edge, market-leading solutions. The associate will work in close collaboration with Power System Services to lead the development and industrial application of advanced AI and computer vision technologies within a commercially focused environment.

The role will require the associate to balance the demands of high-performance computing and advanced research with the practical constraints of industrial deployment. The associate will rapidly develop domain expertise, engage with market and customer requirements, take ownership of key technical activities, and work as an integral member of an established industrial team. The associate will also play a key role in supporting the adoption of new AI-driven methodologies and translating cutting-edge research into practical commercial solutions.

The successful candidate will be a high-calibre, technically driven associate with a PhD in computer vision or a closely related discipline, or equivalent industry experience in the same. They will have strong hands-on experience in rapidly developing and deploying high-performance, technology-driven solutions, together with the ability to translate research and emerging technologies into real-world industrial applications.

 

Main duties and responsibilities

 

Translate complex welding and fabrication challenges into robust AI and imaging solutions suitable for real-world industrial deployment.
Investigate, develop and evaluate machine learning, imaging  and emerging AI technologies to identify effective approaches for the project.
Design, implement and test prototypes, algorithms and software, optimising solutions for real-time performance, computational efficiency, cost and industrial feasibility.
Lead data collection, processing, analysis, and experimentation to train, evaluate, and validate AI models under realistic welding and fabrication conditions.
Develop and implement a framework for effective data collection, processing, analysis and experimentation pipelines for bespoke application contexts.
Study domain and user contexts to determine appropriate domain rules and logic to support the design and development of the solution.
Develop domain expertise in welding and fabrication, engage with end users and stakeholders, and translate operational and market requirements into technical solutions.
Take ownership of multiple parallel activities, including research, rapid prototyping, testing and market analysis, ensuring delivery against project milestones and timelines.
Work closely with the industrial and academic teams to support the adoption of AI-driven methodologies, communicate technical developments, and demonstrate how AI can augment existing expertise and workflows.
Document research and technical outcomes, contribute to reports, presentations and publications, and identify opportunities for innovation, intellectual property and commercial exploitation.
Carry out other duties, commensurate with the remit of the post.

About the Role

We are seeking to appoint a Research Fellow or Project Engineer to assist in the delivery of project milestones and associated scalable deliverables. You will join the team led by Dr Roger Woodman, Human Factors Research Lead (https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/wmg/research/research-areas/human-factors), working closely with the Agritech Team (https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/wmg/for-industry/warwickagritech).

The Innovate UK-funded Agritech project aims to develop Machine Learning for Fault Detection and Predictive Maintenance in Dogtooth’s robotic harvesting systems. Using robot logs, performance data and service records, it will develop explainable AI models to detect faults, predict failures and support targeted maintenance. The project aims to reduce downtime, improve productivity and enable fleet-wide knowledge transfer, while supporting Dogtooth’s commercial scale-up through the SME and ASG teams.

 

Research Fellow

You will research, develop and test AI models for smart automation systems and robotics, covering perception, decision-making, prediction and autonomous control. Working with human factors specialists, you will integrate explainability into machine learning architectures to ensure fault detection and maintenance alerts provide quantitative explanations for technicians and system operators.

You will undertake independent and collaborative research, publish findings in peer-reviewed journals and contribute to research papers. You will also manage project-related administrative challenges, produce regular progress reports and ensure project objectives and deadlines are met.

The role will involve deploying models for real-time, embedded and field-based applications in agricultural environments. This is an opportunity for someone with research experience at the intersection of AI, robotics and human factors.

 

Project Engineer

You will research, develop and test AI models for smart automation systems and robotics, covering perception, decision-making, prediction and autonomous control. Working with the Human Factors Research Lead and cross-functional teams, you will integrate explainability into machine learning architectures, ensuring fault detection and maintenance alerts provide quantitative explanations for field technicians and system operators.

Responsibilities include data collection and processing, developing robust AI systems and deploying models on edge computing devices in real-world agricultural environments. You will also contribute to peer-reviewed journal papers, conference presentations and technical reports.

Both positions are based at the University of Warwick within WMG.

 

For details on the experience and skills required for both positions, please refer to the job description (link here).  

About You

Project Engineer

You should have an honours degree or postgraduate qualification in Computer Science, Data Science, AI or a closely related discipline, supported by a strong mathematical foundation in linear algebra, optimisation and statistics. You will have a strong background in applied AI and machine learning, alongside a demonstrated understanding of Explainable AI (XAI) and human-in-the-loop machine learning methodologies.

You will have effective communication skills, enabling you to report progress to project stakeholders and work collaboratively as part of a team. You will be organised and technically adept, with the ability to initiate, plan, organise, implement and deliver work programmes to tight deadlines.

 

Research Fellow

You should have a PhD-level qualification in Computer Science, Data Science, AI or a closely related discipline, supported by a strong mathematical foundation in linear algebra, optimisation and statistics. You will have a strong background in applied AI and machine learning, alongside a demonstrated understanding of Explainable AI (XAI) and human-in-the-loop methodologies.

You will have effective verbal and written communication skills, enabling you to work with colleagues and external partners and contribute positively to team and School activities. Organised, self-motivated and technically adept, you will confidently use IT to prepare papers, presentations and technical documentation. You will demonstrate good time management, engage constructively with the wider academic community and adopt an inclusive and professional approach.

Candidates who have not yet been awarded their PhD but are nearing submission or have recently submitted may be offered employment as a Research Assistant at level 5 of the University grade structure. Following successful award of the PhD and provision of evidence, they will be promoted to Research Fellow at the first point of level 6.

WMG is the largest department at the University of Warwick, with over 800 staff and nearly 3,000 students across undergraduate and postgraduate programmes in management, technology, and applied engineering.

A fully funded 39 month position is available at the University of Sheffield in the field of Surface engineering & tribology for silicone-free consumer products, funded by EPSRC.

The project aims to decode the fundamental polymer physics/chemistry of lubrication and slip planes across complex, heterogeneous surfaces, using explainable machine learning and materials informatics to rationally design sustainable, high-performance formulations. 

You will be responsible for developing explainable machine learning models (symbolic regression, Bayesian optimisation, and genetic algorithms) to decode polymer-solvent thermodynamics and map soft-matter physics to real world applications. The work is a highly collaborative project between Dr Grant Hill and colleagues within the School of Mathematical and Physical Sciences, and an industrial partner. The project requires a high degree of independence, strong computational skills, and the initiative to bridge theoretical polymer chemistry with experimental data.

Main duties and responsibilities

Algorithm development: Develop and benchmark explainable machine learning models to predict how polymers interact with solvents.

Data integration & featurization: Process and featurize complex polymer architectures to link molecular structure with bulk properties.

About the Role

We are seeking a postdoctoral research fellow to work with us to perform operando electrochemical transmission electron microscopy experiments. You will join the Department of Physics and collaborate with partners in WMG and Chemistry at the University of Warwick. Your role will be to use our operando TEM system (both Protochips and Chipnova electrochemistry holders), analyse resulting data, design suitable electrochemical experiments, and lead your own research projects and will collaborate across interdisciplinary teams using this technique. Beyond driving your own high-impact research, you will have opportunities to help mentor junior group members to develop your broader academic profile. Research topics will principally be in aqueous rechargeable batteries, but will likely include opportunities in rechargeable batteries more broadly as well as other electrochemical systems.

 

For details on the experience and skills required, please refer to the job description (link here).

We are looking for someone who has or will soon obtain a PhD in Chemistry, Materials Science, Physics, or a related discipline. You should have a proven track record of experimental research in advanced transmission electron microscopy, particularly with in situ or operando methods using silicon/silicon nitride microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) chips. Direct experience with liquid cell and electrochemical liquid cell approaches is highly desirable, supported by a firm grounding in electrochemistry and energy materials. In addition, you will have experience in suitable supporting characterisation methods and demonstrated research experience in electrochemistry and electrochemical materials. You should also have a proven track record in academic publishing commensurate with their career stage.

About the role

We are looking for a Research Associate (post-doctoral) to conduct research in AI-enabled process modelling and optimisation, as part of a new collaboration between Repsol S. A. and Imperial College London. We will study two interlinked objectives: (1) the automated generation of dynamic process models using large language models (LLMs), and (2) the data-driven discovery of control strategies trained on those models, focusing on the sim-to-real transfer gap. The work will be validated using real-world industrial case studies and is designed to produce both publishable scientific contributions and deployable engineering/software tools. 

The successful candidate will collaborate with Dr Calvin Tsay in the Department of Computing, along with Dr Antonio del Río Chanona and Dr Mehmet Mercangöz in the Department of Chemical Engineering, and with relevant process modelling teams at Repsol S.A., who will provide access to real-world operating data and case studies. CAMHRA already collaborates with SOAS researchers from Anthropology, Media and Gender Studies. A wider, more epistemically diverse network of researchers across SOAS will help to ensure CAMHRA’s sustainability as a research centre, and support future applications for inter-disciplinary mental health research funding.

MAP-MH@SOAS will systematically identify SOAS researchers who are interested in collaborating with CAMHRA. It will also develop an approach for critically articulating the economic benefit of mental health research, an increasingly important requirement for UKRI funding. Senior PDRA: SOB4ES - The economic value of soil biodiversity and ecosystem services [Full Time, Fixed Term until 3 February 2028]

Join a Horizon funded project that places an economic value on the soil biodiversity beneath our feet. The SOB4ES project runs until 3 February 2028. You will join a small and supportive team led by Prof Simon Jeffery. You will work with Prof Karl Behrendt and Dr Hairong Mu of the Harper Adams Business School. You will also work alongside a PhD student on complementary tasks.

You will lead two high-profile pieces of work. First, you will help to develop a cost-effective framework for estimating the economic value of non-market soil biodiversity contributions to ecosystem services. You will lead the modelling of uncertainty in these values. This will show how the rankings of alternative conservation efforts hold up under different conditions.

Second, you will support the prioritisation of ecosystem services for regional and national soil monitoring programmes and for restoration and conservation planning. You will lead the mapping of priority areas across large spatial scales using the Relative Aggregated Value of Ecosystem Services (RAVES) index. Stakeholder and expert input from project partners will shape the weightings. Your maps will point to the most cost-effective places to invest in soil friendly management.

About the role

How does a compact nervous system combine different sensory cues to make a life-changing decision?

We are seeking a highly motivated Research Associate to join the Chatzigeorgiou Laboratory at Imperial College London and work on a Leverhulme Trust-funded project investigating multisensory decision-making in the larval tunicate Ciona intestinalis. You will examine how mechanical and chemical cues are integrated to control settlement, combining quantitative behaviour, controlled stimulus delivery, whole-brain calcium imaging, neural perturbation and computational analysis. With only 231 neurons and a synaptic-resolution connectome, Ciona offers a powerful opportunity to uncover general principles of sensory integration in a minimal chordate nervous system.

What you would be doing

Lead experiments defining how mechanical and chemical cues interact to regulate larval swimming, settlement and metamorphic commitment in Ciona intestinalis.
Develop high-throughput behavioural assays using millifluidic or microfluidic arenas and quantitative tracking.
Perform whole-brain calcium imaging during precisely controlled unimodal and multimodal stimulation.
Analyse behavioural and imaging datasets to identify nonlinear integration, cue hierarchy and temporal decision dynamics.
Use targeted optogenetic and/or chemogenetic perturbations to test causal circuit mechanisms.
Generate transient transgenic Ciona larvae and contribute to animal culture and experimental workflows.
Publish findings in high-quality international journals and share data and code through open, reproducible workflows.
Present work at national and international conferences and workshops.
Work closely with the PI, students and project collaborators across experimental and modelling work packages.
Help supervise students and contribute to the growth of the Chatzigeorgiou Laboratory at Imperial.

What we are looking for

We are looking for a scientist who has:

A PhD in neuroscience, neurobiology, animal behaviour, physiology, quantitative biology or a closely related discipline.
Evidence of high-quality research and strong publication potential or a publication record appropriate to career stage.
Strong quantitative and analytical skills, with experience in rigorous experimental design and statistical analysis.
Practical experience in fluorescence microscopy, functional imaging and/or calcium imaging.
Practical experience working with an experimental model organism.
Experience in quantitative behavioural analysis and handling complex datasets.
Enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research spanning behaviour, neurobiology, imaging and computation.
Strong communication, organisational and collaborative skills.

Desirable experience includes:

Experience with microfluidics or controlled mechanical and chemical stimulation.
Experience in transgenesis and genetically encoded calcium indicators.
Experience working with Ciona, marine organisms or other non-traditional model systems.
Experience in computer vision or machine learning, such as DeepLabCut, and analysis of calcium-imaging data.

Opportunity to work on an ambitious Leverhulme Trust-funded project addressing fundamental questions in sensory neuroscience, behaviour and evolution.
Access to a uniquely tractable chordate model, whole-brain imaging, controlled-stimulus platforms and connectomic resources, with close interaction between experimental and modelling researchers.
The opportunity to continue your career at a world-leading institution and be part of our mission to continue science for humanity.
Grow your career: gain access to Imperial’s sector-leading dedicated career support for researchers as well as opportunities for promotion and progression.
As a member of research staff you have 10 development days to use to develop your skills and explore your career prospects
Sector-leading salary and remuneration package (including 43 days off a year and generous pension schemes).
Be part of a diverse, inclusive and collaborative work culture with various staff networks and resources to support your personal and professional wellbeing.

About the Role  

About the Role

We are seeking a Research Technician to join Jessica Okosun’s Translational Lymphoma Research group at Barts Cancer Institute. The lab investigates the pathogenesis of lymphomas, investigating tumour heterogeneity/evolution, biomarkers of treatment response and resistance and methodologies to study lymphoma cell populations (Okosun et al Nature Genetics 2016; Araf et al, Leukemia 2018; Coulter et al, J Mol Diagn 2024). The successful applicant will join a collaborative environment accessing clinical trial and tissue bank samples and contribute to molecular biology and omic workflows, including sample processing, storage and NGS library preparation. Working closely with postdoctoral researchers, they will characterize and analyse patient samples and associated data.

About You

The postholder will be an organised, motivated MSc biology (or related discipline) graduate with experience in molecular biology, omics, or flow cytometry. Experience in cancer biology, NGS patient sample handling, or coding is advantageous. Must be detail-oriented, collaborative and keen to learn new techniques.

About the Institute

The BCI is a Cancer Research UK Centre of Excellence whose work aims to transform the lives of those with and at risk of cancer through innovative research in the laboratory, in patients and in populations. It is one of six institutes within The Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry (FMD) BCI is internationally renowned in many areas of cancer research and it combines ground-breaking basic research with the expertise of clinicians and clinician scientists from the Centre for Experimental Cancer Medicine and the Barts NHS Trust to achieve improvements in cancer patient care. BCI is also a partner in the CRUK City of London Major Centre (together with UCL, Kings and the Francis Crick Institute) which is a Centre of Excellence in Biotherapeutics.  BCI is committed in supporting and developing future cancer researchers through its extensive postgraduate training.

About Queen Mary

At Queen Mary University of London, we believe that a diversity of ideas helps us achieve the previously unthinkable.

Throughout our history, we’ve fostered social justice and improved lives through academic excellence. And we continue to live and breathe this spirit today, not because it’s simply ‘the right thing to do’ but for what it helps us achieve and the intellectual brilliance it delivers.

We continue to embrace diversity of thought and opinion in everything we do, in the belief that when views collide, disciplines interact, and perspectives intersect, truly original thought takes form.

We offer competitive salaries, access to a generous pension scheme, 30 days’ leave per annum (pro-rata for part-time/fixed-term), a season ticket loan scheme and access to a comprehensive range of personal and professional development opportunities. In addition, we offer a range of work life balance and family friendly, inclusive employment policies, flexible working arrangements, and campus facilities.

Queen Mary’s commitment to our diverse and inclusive community is embedded in our appointments processes. Reasonable adjustments will be made at each stage of the recruitment process for any candidate with a disability. We are open to considering applications from candidates wishing to work flexibly.

SOAS is moving towards a new model of international partnerships which is responsive to the transnational character of our global challenges.

About the Role

CAMHRA already collaborates with SOAS researchers from Anthropology, Media and Gender Studies. However, we do not have a complete mapping of colleagues across other SOAS departments and schools who work on distress, wellbeing, recovery, displacement, spirituality, care and addiction, perhaps without labelling it as mental health research. A wider, more epistemically diverse network of researchers across SOAS will help to ensure CAMHRA’s sustainability as a research centre, and support future applications for inter-disciplinary mental health research funding.

MAP-MH@SOAS will systematically identify SOAS researchers who are interested in collaborating with CAMHRA. It will also develop an approach for critically articulating the economic benefit of mental health research, an increasingly important requirement for UKRI funding. It will convene two half-day workshops with CAMHRA colleagues to test where collaboration is possible.

WP1: Mapping (December 2026 – May 2027). A research assistant with a critical mental health research background, supervised by Harriet Mossop (CAMHRA R&D Officer), will identify SOAS researchers outside SAMG whose work includes mental health. A long-list will be produced from a systematic, AI-enabled review of researchers’ Worktribe research profiles using key words (distress, wellbeing, etc). A short-list will be compiled from publication abstracts and conversations with researchers.

Outputs: (1) a directory of short-listed researchers giving each researcher's focus, career stage, region, department, methods, and appetite for collaboration. EDI data will be collected with permission.

(2) A visual map ‘MAP-MH@SOAS’ of the cross-SOAS mental health research ecology. (3) A document explaining and mapping this methodology for RKE to use across other research fields. . 

About the Department

CAMHRA, located in the Department of Anthropology, Media and Gender Studies, is funded by a five-year Research England Expanding Excellence grant to develop infrastructure for anthropological research into mental health; the first such infrastructural funding to be received by SOAS. CAMHRA’s discipline-specific research is gaining strong traction with mental health providers, community groups and funders; increasingly, the Centre is also bringing anthropological approaches to collaborative, interdisciplinary work, and embedding

You can find further information on the key criteria for the role in the Job Description and Person Specification, along with a full list of duties and responsibilities, which can be found on the SOAS website

What We Offer:

We are committed to providing a supportive and rewarding work environment. In addition to a competitive salary, we offer a comprehensive range of benefits designed to enhance your well-being and work-life balance:

Generous Holiday Entitlement: Benefit from 44 days of holiday (30 days annual leave, plus bank holidays and 5 closure days over Christmas and Easter) to ensure ample time for rest and relaxation.
Flexible Working Arrangements: We recognise the importance of flexibility and offer options to help you manage your professional and personal commitments effectively.
Generous occupational pension scheme: To provide financial security for your future
Learning and Development: We are dedicated to your professional growth and development and offer diverse learning and development opportunities to enhance your skills and advance your career.
Health and Well-being Initiatives: Take advantage of our cycle to work scheme, eye tests, and season ticket loan to support your health and mobility.
Enhanced Family Leave: We offer enhanced maternity, paternity & partner leave, and shared parental leave to support you during significant life events.
Employee Assistance Programme: Access our confidential EAP for advice and support whenever needed.
Discounted Gym Membership: Maintain your fitness with our discounted gym membership.

How to Apply: 

Please complete the online application form and upload your CV and a supporting statement. 

Closing date: 20th November 2026                               

Interviews to be held: TBC

Further information

Please note that the application system does not currently have a save-and-return feature. To avoid losing any information, we strongly encourage you to complete and submit your application in one sitting. Make sure you have all necessary details ready before you begin.

Successful candidates will need to demonstrate their eligibility to work in the UK or have limited leave to remain in the UK and associated right to work for the duration of their employment with SOAS, in accordance with the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006.

We are not able to offer sponsorship for candidates who do not currently possess the right to work in the UK.

If you have any questions or require any assistance with regard to the application process, please contact us via the HR Contact Form | SOAS

For information on how and why SOAS processes personal data about its job applicants, please read our Job Applicant Notice.

We would particularly welcome applications from candidates from working class, first generation Higher Education, Black, Asian, other minority ethnic and underrepresented groups from within the UK and beyond. All appointment decisions will be made on merit, following a fair and competitive process.

 We are seeking an enthusiastic Research Fellow to join our vibrant research community at the National Oceanography Centre Southampton, University of Southampton, to work on the European Research Council-funded ROSS-SHIFT (Ross Sea Regime Shift) project.

 The successful candidate will investigate potential regime shifts in ocean circulation in the Ross Sea and wider Southern Ocean, and their implications for Antarctic Ice Sheet melting and the Southern Ocean Overturning Circulation. The research will aim to improve our understanding of how changes in ocean circulation and freshwater content influence ocean heat transport towards Antarctic ice shelves, affect their basal melting, and interact with the large-scale overturning circulation. The work will involve the analysis of satellite observations, alongside in situ oceanographic measurements and numerical model outputs, to identify, characterise, and understand changes in Southern Ocean dynamics.

 This position offers an exciting opportunity to contribute to cutting-edge Antarctic research in an international, collaborative environment, with the possibility of participating in Antarctic research cruises. The successful candidate will work closely with collaborators at the British Antarctic Survey, University College London, the University of Gothenburg, the Norwegian Polar Institute and the University of Naples Parthenope.

 We welcome applications from researchers with experience in physical oceanography, satellite remote sensing, ocean observations, numerical modelling, or related disciplines such as mathematics and physics.

 The position is expected to start on 1 March 2027 for an initial period of two years, with the possibility of extension subject to satisfactory progress and funding availability. Some flexibility regarding the start date is available and can be discussed with the successful candidate. For further information or informal enquiries, please contact Dr Alessandro Silvano a.silvano@soton.ac.uk .

 The Department of Politics and International Relations is inviting applications for a position as Research Fellow to conduct research as part of the ESRC-funded project, The International Politics of Soldier Exchanges: Military Families, States and International Institutions .

 The Research Fellow will work closely with Project Co-Lead Dr Natasha Danilova on analysing documents, media and social media coverage pertinent to humanitarian soldier exchanges, and experiences of military families in Russia, using available policy-framing documents, media and social media data sourced from the Integrum database and other relevant sources. Tasks include participating in the creation of a dataset of policy documents that govern the reporting on missing and killed soldiers in Russia; contributing to the analysis of the media coverage of military families across traditional and digital media, including soldiers’ mothers and wives’ protests, and take a lead in the mixed-method analysis of Russia’s military families’ organising on social media and via other digital means.       

 The Research Fellow will co-author relevant research outputs, participate in the training of the project’s staff, and have an opportunity to present preliminary project findings at relevant workshops and conferences.

 The successful candidate will have advanced knowledge and skills in mixed-method, computational/qualitative content analysis (inc. social media data) with expertise on Russia’s politics, gender, war, security and society-military relations. They will be comfortable working across policy documents, traditional mass media, and social media sources, and interested in themes such as military families, gender and feminist analysis of conflicts and conflict-mediation, peace work, humanitarian exchanges, and state-society relations in highly militarized autocratic states.

 This postdoctoral position requires a doctoral degree (or a thesis submitted and awaiting examination) in Politics, International Relations, Peace and Conflict Mediation Studies, Russian Studies, History, or a closely related discipline. The successful candidate will be expected to demonstrate a high level of proficiency in the Russian language.

 Salary will be at the appropriate point on the Grade 6 scale, £39,560 - £40,704 per annum, and negotiable with placement according to qualifications and experience.

 This is a full-time post for 18 months, 1 December 2026 – 31 May 2028.

 Informal enquiries should be made to Dr Natasha Danilova, Senior Lecturer in Politics and International Relations, n.danilova@abdn.ac.uk .

 Please include a cover letter with the application. 

 The closing date for the receipt of applications is 20 November 2026. Interviews will take place in the following week, and the post in place by 1 December 2026. 

 You will be required to complete an online application form. In addition, please supply a full CV and a covering letter (maximum two sides of A4) explaining your fit for the position and addressing the essential and, where possible, desirable criteria. Please do not attach any additional materials, such as writing samples or student evaluations.

 Worldwide, three people are diagnosed with encephalitis every minute—and autoimmune/immune-mediated causes are now just as common as infectious ones. While earlier immunotherapy often resolves acute symptoms like seizures, children remain disproportionately affected by devastating, long-term neuropsychiatric and sleep disorders.

 We are seeking an ambitious Postdoctoral Researcher to join a Wellcome-funded programme bridging this critical research gap. You will use preclinical experimental disease models and advanced electrophysiology to uncover how acute synaptic and neuro-immune disruptions drive persistent brain network changes—and identify new therapeutic targets to improve long-term outcomes for children. Working closely with an embedded clinical research team collecting longitudinal neuroimaging and cognitive data in children and young people, you will form part of a truly translational team.

 Key Responsibilities 

 Drive Translational Discovery: Establish and characterise experimental models of paediatric autoimmune encephalitis to decode the cellular, synaptic, and network mechanisms behind chronic symptoms and test potential therapies.

 Investigate Circuit Function: Perform whole-cell patch clamp and local field potential recordings to uncover synaptic and circuit dysfunction.

 Capture Live Network Activity: Conduct stereotaxic surgeries to implant wireless EEG transmitters and osmotic pumps, analysing in vivo network connectivity and sleep/behavioural phenotypes.

 Explore Neuro-Immune Crosstalk: Investigate how microglia and disrupted neuro-immune signalling drive persistent structural and network changes, contributing to complementary molecular analyses.

 Manage Colony Operations: Oversee a genetically modified colony (breeding, genotyping, and accurate record-keeping) in strict compliance with Home Office regulations.

 Share Impact & Foster a Positive Research Culture: Publish in peer-reviewed journals, present at international conferences, and engage with stakeholders and the public, while supporting a safe, inclusive, and sustainable lab environment. 

 About You 

 You will hold a PhD in neuroscience, physiology, pharmacology, or a related discipline. Strong hands-on experience in in vitro and/or in vivo electrophysiology and stereotaxic surgical techniques is essential, alongside familiarity with UK Home Office regulatory compliance. You bring advanced analytical skills, a collaborative mindset, and a commitment to open, reproducible science.

 What we offer: 

 Aston University is a dynamic and vibrant campus located within Birmingham city centre, which has excellent transport links via bus or train. 

 Excellent training and development opportunities. 

 A generous annual leave scheme with 30 days bookable leave and a further 13 days bank holiday and University Closure days.

 Everyday discounts to a number of activities and retailers

 Great family friendly policies

 On site gym and pool with discounted staff membership available

 Further information on our Benefits and Rewards can be found here 

 This role is likely to qualify for endorsement under the Endorsed Funder route of the Global Talent visa. This visa is for talented or promising individuals in academia or research in fields such as science, engineering, medicine, social sciences, or humanities.

 See the Home Office guidance: https://www.gov.uk/global-talent 

 Closing Date:  23.59 hours GMT on Monday 11 January 2027

 Interview Date:  Friday 29 January 2027

Home  Vacancies  Postdoctoral Researcher in Socio-Technical Resilience & Innovation Management (Fixed Term, 0.6 FTE)
About the role

Bournemouth University is seeking a Postdoctoral Researcher to contribute to MosAIcSOC, a €5.9 million EU-funded project coordinated by BU with 18 partners across Europe. The project is developing a modular, AI-powered Security Operations Centre framework, with applications in critical sectors including healthcare and assisted living.

You will plan, design and conduct socio-technical and human-factors research with security analysts, cybersecurity incident-response teams, healthcare and assisted-living personnel, and technology providers. Your research will inform user requirements and evaluate trust, usability and human decision-making within the project’s pilots. You will contribute to pilot monitoring, data collection and analysis, and the design of crisis simulation exercises examining communication and coordination during incidents. You will produce peer-reviewed publications, project deliverables and reports.

Alongside your research, you will support BU’s role as Project Coordinator through work planning, consortium coordination, European Commission reporting, and risk and quality management. You will also contribute to innovation and intellectual property management, business model analysis, and the sustainability of project outputs, including the SOC App Store and Digital Twin environment.

You will hold a PhD in a relevant discipline by the start date. Essential experience includes research within collaborative EU-funded projects, a proven leadership role in large consortia, and the management and administration of EU-funded projects. You will bring experience of relevant research methods, evidence of peer-reviewed publications, and a strong understanding of research ethics and data integrity. Excellent organisational and interpersonal skills and the ability to work independently and collaboratively are essential.

This position is available on a part-time basis, working 22.2 hours per week (0.6 FTE), for a fixed term between February 2027 to August 2029.

For an informal conversation, please contact Dr Ala Yankouskaya on ayankouskaya@bournemouth.ac.uk

This position does not meet the eligibility requirements for sponsorship under the Skilled Worker Route within the UK Visa and Immigration service’sPoints Based System.  Therefore, BU will not be able to sponsor individuals who require permission to work to carry out this position. For more information, please visit https://www.gov.uk/skilled-worker-visa/your-job. 

 
 
About the department

The post is based in the School of Computing & Engineering within the Faculty of Media, Science & Technology, at BU’s Talbot Campus. You will also work within the BU Cyber Competence Centre, which provides an immersive environment for simulating realistic cyber incidents and exploring AI-supported threat detection, incident response and human decision-making.

The Centre’s emphasis on both technological and human aspects of cyber resilience provides a particularly strong setting for MosAIcSOC, which sits at the intersection of cybersecurity, generative AI and human cognition. Its links with external and industry partners provide opportunities to inform the research through operational cybersecurity challenges and contribute to practical approaches for safer human-AI cyber defence.

Applications are invited for two Postdoctoral Research Associate positions in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics (DAMTP), University of Cambridge, to work with Professor Jorge Santos on "The Microscopic Structure of Black Holes" (MicroBH), a new international project funded by the John Templeton Foundation.

MicroBH brings together four groups with complementary expertise:
- IPhT, CEA Paris-Saclay, France
Prof. Iosif Bena
https://www.ipht.fr/en/string-theory/
- Sapienza University of Rome, Italy
Prof. Paolo Pani
https://gmunu.web.uniroma1.it/

Prof. Jorge Santos

- University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA (lead institution)
Prof. Helvi Witek
https://witek-gravity-group.physics.illinois.edu/

The project aims to connect string theory with gravitational-wave and black-hole observations by constructing the first horizon-scale microstate geometries of astrophysical black holes, evolving their nonlinear dynamics using numerical-relativity simulations, and computing their observable signatures. These include multipole moments, tidal effects, quasinormal modes, echoes, merger waveforms and black-hole images, for comparison with observations from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA and the Event Horizon Telescope, and with the capabilities of future detectors including the Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer and LISA.

Duties include conducting original research in mathematics, developing individual and collaborative research objectives, proposals and projects, and disseminating research findings through presentations and publications. The role holders will be expected to plan and manage their own research activities, contribute to collaborative projects and funding proposals, maintain and develop their specialist knowledge, and communicate complex technical material. They will also be expected to build internal and external networks and contribute to the wider mathematical community. Duties may also include assisting with student project supervision and the development of student research skills, providing limited instruction, and planning and delivering seminars relating to their research area.

The successful candidates will work closely with the principal investigators and their groups across all four institutions through working visits, annual in-person network meetings and regular remote meetings. They will be expected to participate in network activities, contribute to organising a cross-community PhD school and workshops, and support the training of students.

Candidates must hold, or be about to complete, a PhD in Physics or a related field. Applicants with expertise in string theory and supergravity, black-hole physics, numerical relativity, numerical methods for partial differential equations, or gravitational-wave modelling and phenomenology are particularly encouraged to apply.

These posts form part of the wider MicroBH recruitment of eight postdoctoral researchers, with two based at each partner institution. Further information about the joint call can be found here: https://academicjobsonline.org/ajo/jobs/33404.

Fixed-term: The funds for this post are available for 2 years in the first instance. An extension may be possible, subject to the availability of funds.

Expected start date: August or September 2027. Earlier start dates may be considered.

Closing date: 15 December 2026. Screening of applications will begin in December 2026.

Click the 'Apply' button below to register an account with our recruitment system (if you have not already) and apply online.

Applicants are requested to submit:
1. a cover letter;
2. a curriculum vitae, including a list of publications;
3. a research statement of no more than three pages, using one-inch margins and a font size of 11 to 12 points, outlining previous and current research and future research plans;
4. contact details, including email addresses, for three academic referees who will be asked to provide letters of recommendation.

Please ensure that at least one referee is contactable throughout the selection process. Referees should be aware that the Mathematics HR Office Administrator may contact them to request a reference through the University's Web Recruitment System, and they should be encouraged to respond promptly.

Informal enquiries about the project may be directed to microBH@uniroma1.it.

If you have any queries regarding the application process, please email us at LE51646@maths.cam.ac.uk.

Please quote reference LE51646 on your application and in any correspondence about this vacancy.

For evolutionary biology to provide solutions to contemporary issues in human society, conservation biology, and medicine, evolution must be predictable. But whether species evolve repeatable molecular solutions to common adaptive challenges remains an open question. Sex and aging represent two of the most consistent challenges for multicellular life, with dynamic consequences for population viability and health. Extant species have successfully navigated cooperation, conflict, and resolution between sexes and age-classes, where convergent molecular adaptations offer valuable potential solutions to challenges in conservation biology and human health. By evaluating sex- and age-specific fitness across ten independent Drosophila lineages spanning 1–70 million years of divergence, this project will reveal whether evolution has predictable genomic feaures, and why or why not.

Expertise in read mapping, allele frequency estimation from pooled sequencing (Pool-seq), statistical genetics, phylogenetic comparative methods, or experience with Drosophila would be particularly beneficial. About the role

Early detection of oral cancer, particularly oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), is critical to improving patient outcomes and survival rates. When diagnosed at an early stage, the five-year survival rate exceeds 80%; however, this falls to below 50% when the disease is diagnosed at more advanced stages (III–IV). Despite the accessibility of the oral cavity and the potential for individuals to recognise early changes, nearly half of oral cancer cases in the UK are still diagnosed at an advanced stage. This highlights an urgent need for innovative, accessible and reliable diagnostic tools to support earlier detection and intervention.

We are seeking a motivated and enthusiastic researcher to contribute to the development of a prototype diagnostic test kit capable of detecting cancer-specific biomarkers associated with oral cancer. The overarching aim of this research is to develop a sensitive, reliable and potentially accessible detection platform that could facilitate earlier diagnosis and ultimately improve patient outcomes.

The successful candidate will undertake experimental research involving the chemical synthesis, characterisation and analytical evaluation of biomarker detection components. The role will involve developing and optimising detection strategies, assessing their performance, and contributing to the design and validation of a prototype test kit. The postholder will also be expected to analyse and interpret experimental data, maintain accurate research records, and contribute to the preparation of scientific reports, publications and presentations.

This is an exciting opportunity to contribute to interdisciplinary research at the interface of chemistry, analytical science and cancer diagnostics, with the potential to make a meaningful impact on the early detection of oral cancer.

About us

The British Election Study is the longest-running and most authoritative survey of electoral behaviour in the UK, tracking the attitudes and behaviour of British voters at every general election since 1964. 

Royal Holloway with King's College London and the University of Manchester have been awarded £4.9million by the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) to lead the British Election Study (BES) for the next five years (2027-2032). During this period, the team will introduce new methods, new data and new ways of making the BES accessible to researchers, policymakers, journalists and the public.

Within the BES project, the Department of Informatics at King’s College London is responsible for developing the BES’s Artificial Intelligence Interface (the BES-AII). Integrated into the BES website (https://www.britishelectionstudy.com/), the BES-AII will offer users the opportunity to access and interact with BES data through natural language queries, making the BES data more accessible to non-specialist users than ever before.

About the role

The Department of Informatics at King’s College London is seeking to appoint a Postdoctoral Researcher to lead the development and maintenance of the British Election Study’s public facing AI Interface (BES-AII).

The researcher will be responsible for upgrading the BES’s data infrastructure, including harmonising data across survey waves, and will collaborate with other members of the BES team (largely political scientists) to develop a knowledge base (ontology) for the BES, which will support the mapping of related BES survey questions, political concepts, and third-party political data.

Building on the BES data infrastructure and knowledge base, the researcher will lead the development of the BES-AII where users can interact with and export BES data using natural language queries. The system will initially build on an existing data retrieval architecture using Retrieval Augmented Generation and will then move towards using more advanced tools which combine large language models and knowledge bases (e.g., LLM-Wiki - https://llm-wiki.net/). We also expect that the researcher will play a small role in supporting the collection and analysis of donated social media data from BES survey respondents, if required.

Throughout the project, the researcher will contribute to outreach activities, will support extensive (AI) safety testing, and will contribute to ensuring that the BES maintains its duty to remain politically impartial.

The role is primarily focused on research software development, but we anticipate additional opportunities for the researcher to contribute to computational social science and AI safety research using BES data.

The researcher will be based in the Department of Informatics and will report to Dr Max Falkenberg (primary supervisor), and Professor Rosie Campbell (second supervisor; political science lead for the BES at KCL).

The Role

 

We are delighted to launch an exciting new opportunity for a Research Assistant /Research Associate in Novel Proteins for Animal Feeds and Nutrition to join us in the School of Natural and Environmental Science, Newcastle University, United Kingdom as detailed below:

 

Most chicken feed in the UK currently relies on imported soya as a source of protein, which is expensive, vulnerable to global disruptions and linked to deforestation and high carbon emissions. Newcastle University is a lead partner of an InnovateUK-DEFRA funded, multi-partner project exploring how UK-grown blue lupins can replace part of the soya used in broiler chicken diets.

 

We are seeking a driven and enthusiastic individual to join our team and contribute to this research, leading on the delivery, analysis and reporting of feed trials with broliers to ensure that blue lupin inclusion in diets maintains bird health, productivity and welfare.

 

 Feed trials will be run within Newcastle University’s state of the art Animal Science Facilities with the support of dedicated academic and technical staff involved in the project. The successful candidate will input into trial planning/preparation and subsequent daily maintainance activities and weekly assessments of ethically approved number of birds over pre-determined starter-grower-finisher cycles. Video recordings taken over the trial durations will be processed by the project RA to provide data on bird welfare/health/behaviour. The successful candidate will lead on assessments and data analysis/reporting, as well as the publication of trial outputs and the dissemination of results at project meetings, and more widely at conferences/events. 

 

You will join an experienced team at Newcastle University, led by Dr Abdul Chaudhry (abdul.chaudhry@newcastle.ac.uk) as the Principal Investigator. They will join the Agriculture and Food Systems Group within the School of Natural & Environmental Sciences, also linking to the wider project consortium which includes key industry growers, suppliers and processors.

 We are seeking an outstanding computational biologist to join the BioFAIR Pathfinder project to develop computational framework for gene regulatory network (GRN) inference methods in single-cell genomics.

 The project involves curating, harmonising single-cell and multimodal datasets, containerising and running, comparing GRN inference tools as a community resource. The role includes contributing to peer-reviewed publications and developing community, training and engagement opportunities with BioFAIR and ELIXIR-UK Southampton node.

ABOUT THE UNIVERSITY

Swansea University is a research-led university that has been making a difference since 1920. The University community thrives on exploration and discovery and offers the right balance of excellent teaching and research, matched by an enviable quality of life.

Our stunning waterfront campuses and multicultural community make us a desirable workplace for colleagues from around the world. Our reward and benefits, and ways of working enable those who join us to have enriching careers, matched by an excellent work-life balance.

ABOUT THE ROLE

The PDRA will join the research programme led by Prof. M. Piai, applying lattice field theory techniques and numerical implementations to new strongly coupled realizations of composite dynamics and its applications, with particular reference to the TELOS collaboration. Specific scientific goals will be codesigned, and involve a combination of software development, testing and benchmarking on high performance computing facilities, as well as on physics analysis pertinent to one or more of the physics aims and objectives of the collaboration.

The ideal candidate for the post has a strong background in programming and running lattice calculations on modern, parallel computing facilities, using both CPU and GPU architecture, as well as previous experience with theoretical particle physics. Familiarity with current trends in extensions of the Standard Model is desirable, as is expertise with effective field theory techniques, and with more formal theoretical ideas, such as those of gauge/gravity dualities. The project will include both a software development component and a physics analysis one, hence candidates are invited to provide in their application technical details about their previous experience on both aspects.

The candidate is expected to take active part in the TELOS collaboration, committing to its the research aims and objectives, professional values, and code of conduct, including its open access, open data and open software policies. They will have the opportunity to co-supervise the research aspects of the activity of postgraduate research students. They will participate to the activities of the Centre for Quantum Fields and Gravity, including attending and organising seminars in the broad context of theoretical particle physics.

The appointment is for 1 year full-time, but can be converted into a part-time appointment (50%) for two years. Extension to a third year might become possible in principle, if additional funding becomes available, and pending performance review.

Contract - 1 October 2027-30 September 2028

The University is committed to supporting and promoting equality and diversity in all its practices and activities. As an inclusive and welcoming workplace, we value people for their skills regardless of their background. Applications are welcome in Welsh and will not be treated less favourably than those submitted in English.

WELSH LANGUAGE SKILLS

The Welsh language level required for this role is Level 1 - A little. The role holder will be able to pronounce Welsh words, answer the phone in Welsh (good morning/afternoon) and use very basic everyday words and phrases (thank you, please etc.). Level 1 can be reached by completing a 1 hour course.

The University is a proud bilingual institution, our Welsh Language Strategy outlines our aspiration to promote the language and enable our staff to engage with the language as an additional workplace skill and as a gateway to new cultural and social opportunities. Applications are welcome in Welsh and will not be treated less favourably than those submitted in English. Welsh speakers have the right to an interview in Welsh. Applicants for a role where Welsh skills are essential are expected to present their application in Welsh and will be interviewed in Welsh, if shortlisted.

Piai, applying lattice field theory techniques and numerical implementations to new strongly coupled realizations of composite dynamics and its applications, with particular reference to the TELOS collaboration. Specific scientific goals will be codesigned, and may include for example composite Higgs models, dilaton-Higgs models, top partial compositeness, quasi-conformal dynamics, strongly interacting models of dark matter.

The ideal candidate for the post has a strong background in theoretical particle physics, and previous experience with programming and running lattice calculations on modern, parallel computing facilities, using both CPU and GPU architecture. Familiarity with current trends in extensions of the Standard Model is desirable, as is expertise with effective field theory techniques, and with more formal theoretical ideas, such as those of gauge/gravity dualities. The project will include both a software development component and a physics analysis one, hence candidates are invited to provide in their application technical details about their previous experience on both aspects.

The candidate is expected to take active part in the TELOS collaboration, committing to its the research aims and objectives, professional values, and code of conduct, including its open access, open data and open software policies. They will have the opportunity to co-supervise the research aspects of the activity of postgraduate research  students. They will participate to the activities of the Centre for Quantum Fields and Gravity, including attending and organising seminars in the broad context of theoretical particle physics.

The appointment is for 2 years full-time.  Extension to a third year might become possible in principle, if additional funding becomes available, and pending performance review.

EQUALITY, DIVERSITY & INCLUSION

The University is committed to supporting and promoting equality and diversity in all its practices and activities. We aim to establish an inclusive environment and welcome diverse applications from the following protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race (including colour, nationality, ethnic and national origin), religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

As an inclusive and welcoming workplace, we value people for their skills regardless of their background. Applications are welcome in Welsh and will not be treated less favourably than those submitted in English.

WELSH LANGUAGE SKILLS

The Welsh language level required for this role is Level 1 - A little. The role holder will be able to pronounce Welsh words, answer the phone in Welsh (good morning/afternoon) and use very basic everyday words and phrases (thank you, please etc.). Level 1 can be reached by completing a 1 hour course.

The University is a proud bilingual institution, our Welsh Language Strategy outlines our aspiration to promote the language and enable our staff to engage with the language as an additional workplace skill and as a gateway to new cultural and social opportunities. Applications are welcome in Welsh and will not be treated less favourably than those submitted in English. Welsh speakers have the right to an interview in Welsh. Applicants for a role where Welsh skills are essential are expected to present their application in Welsh and will be interviewed in Welsh, if shortlisted.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

 About us 

 The Cell and Tissue biophysics lab, headed by Prof Guillaume Charras, focuses on the role of cytoskeletal organisation and adhesion in the mechanics of cells and tissues. A particular interest is to understand the cycle of feedback between geometry, differentiation and mechanical changes that shape tissues during morphogenesis.

 In our research, we combine analytical and characterisation techniques from physics and engineering with molecular cell biology techniques and optical microscopy to study questions relevant to cell and developmental biology. We interact closely with the Institute for the Physics of Living Systems, a vibrant scientific community. IPLS is a cross-faculty initiative at UCL that brings together researchers from the life sciences, physics, engineering, and mathematics to study the physical principles underlying Life.

 The London Centre for Nanotechnology (LCN) is an interdisciplinary enterprise between University College London, King’s College London and Imperial College London. In bringing together world-class infrastructure and leading nanotechnology research activities, the Centre aims to attain the critical mass to compete with the best facilities abroad. The LCN has strong relationships with the broader nanotechnology and commercial communities, and is involved in much major collaboration. As the world’s only such facility to be located in the heart of a metropolis, the LCN has superb access to corporate, investment and industrial partners. It is at the forefront of training in nanotechnology, and has a strong media presence aimed at educating the public and bringing transparency to this emerging science.

 About the role 

 This position is part of an interdisciplinary collaborative project between the Francis Crick Institute, the University of Warwick, the University of Edinburgh and UCL. The aim of the project is to understand the principles that underlie the acquisition and organisation of tissue shape in organoids. Self-organisation necessitates a symmetry-breaking event that causes gene expression changes in a subpopulation of cells, resulting in changes in molecular and mechanical properties that shape the form and function of tissues. This process is iterative. As new contacts form between cells of different lineages, as some cells lose contact with the extracellular matrix, and as new secreted molecules are produced, further rounds of organisation take place. Thus, predicting the outcome of morphogenesis lies at the interface between physics and biology as it involves cycles of changes in mechanics and gene expression that feedback across multiple spatiotemporal s cales. Our team will integrate physics and biological perspectives to understand and to predict how cycles of gene expression and mechanical changes give rise to complex morphogenesis of tissues and organs over a duration of several days.

 In this project, we propose to determine how cell differentiation and cellular-scale mechanical changes combine to control shape acquisition using organoids generated in vitro from embryonic stem cells (neuruloids). This is an attractive system to reverse engineer as neuruloids reproducibly acquire complex tissue shapes and comprise multiple cell-types but remain sufficiently simple to allow spatiotemporal characterisation of cell morphology, mechanics, differentiation and gene expression. We will determine how mechanics, adhesion, and gene expression interplay at the cell-scale to guide shape acquisition at the tissue-scale.
